task: apply for a government benefit online or manage an existing claim (unemployment insurance, SNAP/food stamps, disability, Medicaid, housing assistance — state portals and agency sites): work through the eligibility screens and application form and submit, or certify/check an existing claim; complete when the submission confirmation or the claim-status screen is shown. Surface pinned: the government benefits portal itself — not benefit-explainer talking heads without a portal session.

tree.label: Claim a government benefit
tree.note: 1 then 2 every session. then the session's job: 3 once per claim, 4 every week the claim lives, 5 when certifying lapses, 8 once benefits flow onto the card. 6 closes 3, 4, and 5; 7 follows 6. the jobs chain across sessions - 3's confirmation starts the clock on 4, and 4 stays blocked while 5 processes (76Pa).

children.note: 1.1 and 1.2 in either order; 1.3 and 1.4 before committing to the session - 1.4 can end it before it starts (iVa7's outage window). then 1.5. certifiers re-enter here every week.

children.label: Establish the account
children.note: 2.1 decides the wall: sign in (2.4), register (2.2, sometimes on the agency, sometimes on Login.gov or ID.me - the evidence notes say which), or guest past a CAPTCHA (q2an; 8v-j allows guest for one program only). 2.3 where the agency demands proofing - D3uH and o9iF are entire sessions inside this goal, and CA and AZ interpose it mid-application (a0_z, 5P67).

questions.question: Did your account creation succeed, and are you now viewing the main dashboard?
questions.why: Confirming the 'my Social Security' dashboard loads ensures your account was created properly and displays your initial eligibility and work credits.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You miss seeing your immediate eligibility status, work credits summary, and any urgent unread messages upon first logging in.

questions.why: If someone else fraudulently used your SSN, or if you have an old forgotten account, the system will hard-stop the process.

questions.check: Which ways in does the page offer: sign in, create an account, or continue without one?

children.note: 2.2.1 then 2.2.2; 2.2.3 and 2.2.4 where the portal uses them; 2.2.5 where a confirmation email closes the loop; 2.2.6 wherever the form plants one. Or9Z fills everything and deliberately never submits - the narrator already has an account.

questions.why: The Terms of Service explicitly forbid using an account created by another person or operating it on someone else's behalf, even with written permission.

questions.check: Do the terms state the account must be created and operated by the person themselves, not by another on their behalf?

questions.check: Which payment methods does the page offer?
questions.say_example: How do you want the money? Straight to your bank, or their prepaid card? The card comes with fees. Deposit needs your account and routing numbers.

questions.question: Did the system reject your bank's routing number, forcing you to either provide a different account or accept a fee-heavy prepaid debit card?
questions.why: Legacy state systems frequently reject routing numbers from smaller credit unions or newer online banks, which can automatically default your payment method to a state-issued debit card.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the opportunity to provide an alternative bank account, potentially getting locked into a prepaid card that charges ATM and maintenance fees.
questions.check: Does the page show the routing number was rejected?
questions.say_example: The site rejected your bank's routing number. It happens with <online banks>. Another account, or the prepaid card? The card charges <ATM and inactivity> fees.

questions.question: Are you comfortable with the fees and terms associated with the debit card payment option?
questions.why: The screen displays the U.S. Bank ReliaCard fee disclosure, detailing potential costs like out-of-network ATM and inactivity fees that will affect your benefit funds.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the chance to personally evaluate the debit card's fee structure and decide if another payment method might save you money.
questions.check: Which fees does the card disclosure list?
questions.say_example: The card's fee sheet: <out-of-network ATM 1.25, inactivity 2 a month>. Direct deposit has none of these. Still want the card?

questions.question: Do you want federal and state taxes withheld from your benefit payments?
questions.why: This determines whether taxes are deducted directly from your benefits, which affects both your immediate payout amount and your end-of-year tax liability.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: Letting an agent make this choice means losing control over your personal tax strategy and the net amount of your immediate benefit payments.
questions.check: Does the page offer withholding federal and state taxes from payments?
questions.say_example: Want taxes taken out as you go? It's <10 percent> off each payment now, or a bill at tax time. Most people say withhold.

questions.question: Did the screen confirm the notice preferences were saved before continuing back to the account home page?
questions.why: The screen confirms your preferences were successfully updated and provides a button to continue to your my Social Security homepage.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the immediate visual confirmation that your account preferences were saved correctly before entering the main portal.
questions.check: Does the page confirm preferences were updated and offer a continue button?
questions.say_example: Preferences saved. Went on to the homepage.

questions.question: How do you want to receive notices from Social Security?
questions.why: You must choose whether to receive only secure online notices or both paper and online notices before saving and continuing.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: Delegating this means you lose the ability to decide whether you receive important physical mail or only digital communications from Social Security.
questions.check: Which notice delivery options does the page offer?
questions.say_example: Where should legal notices go: online only, or paper too? A missed notice can quietly close an appeal window. Which do you want?

questions.question: Do you want to backdate this claim, and if so, to what date and for what reason?
questions.why: The system requires a specific effective date and a written explanation if you choose to backdate your unemployment claim.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the ability to provide their specific personal justification for the delayed filing, which is required to process the backdate request.
questions.check: Does the page offer backdating the claim with a date and reason?
questions.say_example: Your job ended <weeks ago> but the claim would start this week. The form can backdate it with a reason. Want me to ask for <the earlier date>? The reason I'd give: <what you told me happened>.

questions.question: Did the application let you proceed to the next screen without filling in the required reason for backdating?
questions.why: The system advanced to the Employer screen even though the field marked with an asterisk for backdating the claim was left blank.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the opportunity to ensure their application is fully complete, risking a delay or denial if the agency later flags the missing explanation.
questions.check: Did the page advance while the required backdate reason was blank?
questions.say_example: The page let us through with the backdate reason empty, required mark and all. If it went through blank the claim may start on the wrong week. Going back to fill it.

questions.question: Which of the suggested documents do you want to upload now?
questions.why: The screen lists suggested documents like proof of income that you can upload now, though it notes you can still submit the application without them.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the chance to decide whether to gather and provide these documents immediately or wait for the eligibility worker to require them.
questions.check: Which documents does the page suggest or require uploading?
questions.say_example: The page wants <proof of income>, a pay stub or a tax form. You can skip it, but the review slows until they get it. Do you have one for me, or skip?

questions.question: Did the system reject your document upload due to a file size or format error, allowing you to proceed but guaranteeing a manual review delay?
questions.why: State portals often have archaic file constraints (e.g., 2MB PDF only). If an upload fails, the system may still let you click 'Next', but your claim will be delayed for missing evidence.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the awareness that their critical proof of income or ID was never actually attached, leading to a surprise denial or weeks of delay.
questions.check: Does the page show an upload error naming a size or format limit?
questions.say_example: The upload bounced. The site only takes <PDFs under 2 megabytes>. I'm shrinking it and trying again.

questions.question: Does the visual thumbnail preview of the uploaded document show that the image is legible and not cut off?
questions.why: After selecting a file, the portal usually displays a small visual preview to confirm what was attached before you submit the form.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The agent might attach a file, but without seeing the visual preview, the user cannot verify if the image is blurry, cropped, or the wrong document entirely, which would lead to a rejected claim.
questions.check: Does the uploaded document's preview show the full page, readable?
questions.say_example: The preview of your <pay stub> is cut off. The amounts don't show. Re-uploading a full shot so it counts.

questions.question: Did the portal display a success icon or thumbnail confirming the document was fully uploaded?
questions.why: The only way to know a file attached correctly before submitting is often a visual indicator like a green checkmark, a completed progress bar, or a small preview image.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The agent might click 'next' without verifying the visual success state, potentially submitting a blank or corrupted file that will cause the claim to be delayed or denied.
questions.check: Does the page show a success mark or thumbnail for the uploaded file?
questions.say_example: Uploaded <the pay stub>. The page shows it attached.

children.label: Certify a claim week
children.note: 4.1, then 4.2 and 4.3 as the portal interposes them. 4.4, with 4.5 where a No on earnings spawns it; 4.6 as the state requires. repeat 4.4 to 4.6 once per claim week in the session - lVpW and urAf each run two. 4.7 rides on the final week only. 6 closes it.

questions.question: Are there weeks available to certify for benefits, and what is the deadline?
questions.why: The dashboard notification indicates you have weeks available to certify and warns that missing the specified deadline could affect your eligibility.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose direct visibility into your current claim balance and the exact deadline required to keep your benefits active.
questions.check: Which weeks does the page show available to certify, and by when?
questions.say_example: Two weeks are ready to certify, <the 8th through the 21st>. The deadline is <Saturday>. Starting now.

questions.question: Should you read the detailed eligibility text before clicking the 'Certify for Benefits' button?
questions.why: The screen displays detailed eligibility information below the notification box that could contain important requirements or updates for your claim.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the opportunity to personally review the specific eligibility criteria presented on the screen before initiating the certification process.
questions.check: Does the page show eligibility text near the certify button?
questions.say_example: Read the eligibility notes before starting. Nothing new for you.

questions.question: Do you need to file a new weekly certification to continue your claim?
questions.why: The screen displays your previously submitted weeks as 'In Progress' and provides a button to file for the next week to maintain your benefits.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the chance to personally review the status of your recent payouts before initiating the next weekly claim.
questions.check: Does the page show a button to file the next weekly certification?
questions.say_example: Filed the next week, like you asked.

questions.question: Which specific time period am I answering these certification questions for?
questions.why: The screen shows a slight date discrepancy between the week header and the instruction text, so you must confirm the exact dates you are certifying for before answering.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the opportunity to personally verify the exact dates of the certification week and catch the minor date discrepancy on the form.
questions.check: What week do the header and the instruction text each name?
questions.say_example: The page header says the week of <one date>, the instructions say <another>. Answers are sworn per week, so I'm confirming which it means before answering.

questions.question: What fraud rules must I acknowledge to proceed?
questions.why: You must check the box to confirm you understand the penalties for fraud, such as failing to report new earnings, before you can continue.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the chance to personally review the specific legal obligations and fraud penalties you are being held accountable for.
questions.check: What does the page require acknowledging about fraud and reporting earnings?
questions.say_example: This page makes you confirm the fraud rules. The one that trips people: work counts the week you do it, not when the pay lands. I've confirmed, and it's in my report.

questions.question: Should you read the payment processing details before clicking continue?
questions.why: The page contains important details about direct deposit and processing times, such as a five-day wait, that affect how and when you receive your benefits.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the opportunity to understand the timeline for receiving your funds and the rules for updating your banking information.
questions.check: What does the page say about payment processing times?
questions.say_example: Payments run about <five days> after certifying. It's in my report.

questions.question: Do you have the required information ready to complete your weekly certification?
questions.why: Reviewing the 'What You Will Need' and 'Important To Know' sections ensures you have the correct details ready before starting the questionnaire.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You miss reading the specific requirements and important rules that govern your weekly claim.
questions.check: What does the page list as needed for the weekly certification?
questions.say_example: Checked the needed-info list. We have it all.

questions.question: What filing window does the page state, and is it open now?
questions.why: The guidelines explicitly state that weekly claim certifications must be filed between 12:01 am Sunday and 11:59 pm on Saturday to be accepted.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the awareness of the strict weekly filing window, which could result in them missing the deadline and losing their benefits for that week if the agent delays the submission.
questions.check: What filing window does the page state, and is the current time inside it?
questions.say_example: Certifications are only accepted <Sunday through Saturday> for last week. It's outside that window now. Filing when it opens <Sunday>.

questions.question: Is your contact information correct, or do you need to update it?
questions.why: The screen explicitly warns that you must keep your contact information current, requiring you to verify the displayed address, phone, and email before continuing.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the opportunity to verify that the agency has your most up-to-date address and phone number for critical benefit communications.
questions.check: What address, phone, and email does the page display?
questions.say_example: The page still has your old <address>. Money and letters go there. Updating it to <the current one> first.

questions.question: How should I answer the weekly certification questions about my availability, work search, and earnings?
questions.why: Accurately answering these specific questions about sickness, work search, and earnings is required to determine your continued eligibility for weekly benefits.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: Delegating this step means the agent might incorrectly report your personal work search efforts or earnings for the week, potentially risking your benefits or triggering fraud flags.
questions.check: Which certification questions does the page ask for this week?
questions.say_example: The week's questions are about your life, so they're yours to answer. There are <seven>. First: <did you do any work between the 8th and the 14th>?

questions.question: Are the pre-filled answers to the weekly eligibility questions correct for your situation?
questions.why: You must verify that the answers regarding whether you worked, refused work, or received a pension during the specified week are accurate before proceeding.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the chance to personally verify your weekly activities and income, risking an inaccurate claim being submitted on your behalf.
questions.check: Which answers does the page show already filled before any were entered?
questions.say_example: The form came with answers already in it. It says <you didn't work>. Pre-filled isn't answered. Confirm each one before I keep it.

questions.question: Does the page flag any question as unanswered?
questions.why: Leaving any mandatory radio buttons blank will trigger an error and prevent you from advancing to the work search record.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the chance to personally verify that your specific answers accurately reflect your situation for the certification week.
questions.check: Does the page flag required questions as unanswered?
questions.say_example: All questions answered. Nothing flagged.

children.label: Prove the work search
children.note: the state sets the shape: 4.6.1 where the rules need reading; repeat 4.6.2 until the quota holds (iVa7 needs three that count, 2mL- three when the activities are applications); 4.6.3 where the log arrives pre-filled; 4.6.4 where the page invites its own bypassing. absent entirely for some claim types - Jt5q answers a question instead, and xoKC has no log step yet certifies work-search activities at 6.4.

questions.question: Do you need to add more job contacts to meet the weekly minimum?
questions.why: The screen warns that you must report at least three job contacts per week or your unemployment benefit payment may be denied.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: Delegating this step means you lose the ability to accurately report your specific job search efforts to ensure your benefits are approved.
questions.check: How many work-search contacts does the page count as valid, and how many does it require?
questions.say_example: Only <2> job contacts count for the week. One got a red mark, looking isn't contacting. The page wants <3> or the payment can be denied. Who else did you apply to?

questions.question: Do you need to review the help text to understand what qualifies as looking for work?
questions.why: The 'UI Online Help' window provides specific definitions for what counts as looking for work, ensuring you answer the eligibility question accurately.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the chance to personally review the agency's specific definitions to ensure your recent activities actually qualify.
questions.check: Does the page provide help text defining what counts as looking for work?
questions.say_example: Read their definition of a work search before logging yours.

questions.question: What are the application details for this job contact?
questions.why: The screen requires you to specify your interest level, whether you contacted the employer, the date, and the contact method to log your work search activity.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to accurately report the specific dates and methods of your personal job search efforts.
questions.check: Which fields does the work-search entry form require?
questions.say_example: I need this week's job contacts, <three> of them. For each: the employer, the date, and how you applied. Who's first?

questions.question: Are your logged work search methods valid despite the warning to only use the Reemployment Exchange?
questions.why: An on-screen caption explicitly requires using the Reemployment Exchange, but the system's log shows that 'In Person' and 'EMail' contacts were accepted.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the opportunity to clarify if their alternative work search methods will ultimately be rejected and cause a claim denial despite appearing accepted in the log.
questions.check: Does the page restrict which search methods count, and which methods does the log show?
questions.say_example: The page says only <Reemployment Exchange> searches count, but it accepted your <in person> ones. If it means the rule, those may not count. Worth adding one through <the Exchange> to be safe.

questions.question: Do you need to provide work search details for this week?
questions.why: The screen provides an option to bypass the work search entry by clicking 'Next', which is important to notice if your specific employment status exempts you from this requirement.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: Delegating this step means an agent might incorrectly skip or fabricate work search records without knowing your actual exemption status or weekly activities.
questions.check: Does the page allow proceeding without work-search entries?
questions.say_example: Skipped the work-search page. Your <recall date> exempts you this week.

questions.question: Do you want to withhold taxes from this week's payment or update your contact information?
questions.why: The weekly certification form includes optional questions asking if you want federal taxes withheld from your payment or if you need to update your mailing address.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: Delegating this step means you lose direct control over your tax withholding preferences and the opportunity to ensure your contact details are current.
questions.check: Does the page ask about withholding and contact updates this week?
questions.say_example: Kept your standing choices: taxes withheld, contact details unchanged.

children.label: Reopen the claim
children.note: 5.1 - an expired claim exits to a new application through 3, and employer-issued claim forms exit to the phone. then 5.2, 5.3, 5.4; 6 closes it. 4 stays blocked until the request processes.

children.label: Read the claim status and choose the path

questions.question: Do I need to reopen my claim based on my current notifications?
questions.why: The screen shows a notification that you haven't certified recently and must click the button to reopen your claim.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: Delegating this step means you miss seeing the specific reason your claim was paused and the special instructions regarding employer or union claim forms.
questions.check: Does the page say the claim must be reopened before certifying?
questions.say_example: The claim went quiet too long, and the page wants it reopened before anything pays. Doing that now. It re-asks a few eligibility questions.

questions.question: Has your claim expired, requiring you to file a new claim instead of reopening the old one?
questions.why: The dashboard notification explicitly states the claim has expired, which changes the required action from simply certifying or reopening to filing a completely new claim.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: An agent might try to certify for weeks on an expired claim, wasting time or causing confusion, instead of realizing a new application is required.
questions.check: Does the page say the claim has expired and a new one is required?
questions.say_example: The claim expired <last month>. Reopening isn't offered. It has to be a fresh claim, and the weekly amount can come out different. Want me to start one?

questions.question: How should you answer the eligibility questions regarding other income and specific employment situations?
questions.why: The application requires you to declare any expected Workers' Compensation or other employer income and clarify if your unemployment is due to a trade dispute to determine your benefit eligibility.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: Delegating this means the agent might incorrectly report your other income sources or mischaracterize the exact reason for your unemployment, potentially jeopardizing your claim.
questions.check: Which eligibility questions does the reopen flow ask?
questions.say_example: Reopening asks a few things only you know: <expecting workers' comp, any strike at your job, a union claim form>. I'll read them one at a time.

questions.question: Should you save your application as a draft to finish later?
questions.why: The narrator explains that clicking the 'Save as Draft' button preserves your progress until Saturday at 11:59 pm PST if you need to step away to gather more information.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to decide when to pause the application and the awareness of the strict Saturday deadline to resume before your data is deleted.
questions.check: Does the page offer saving the application as a draft?
questions.say_example: No need for the draft button. We finished in one sitting.

questions.question: Does the page show a saved-draft confirmation?
questions.why: The narrator mentions saving progress, but the video skips directly to a login screen without showing the button being clicked or a success message.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the certainty that their application progress was actually saved before the session was interrupted.
questions.check: Does the page show a saved-draft confirmation?
questions.say_example: Saved a draft and the page confirmed it before I stepped away.

children.label: Identify the last employer from the records

questions.question: Which employer from the provided list should I select as my last employer?
questions.why: The agency requires you to accurately identify the very last employer you performed work for, regardless of whether the job was full-time, part-time, or temporary.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to ensure the exact final employer is selected, which is critical if you recently juggled multiple temporary or part-time jobs that an agent might confuse.
questions.check: Which employers does the page list from state records, and does one match the person's?
questions.say_example: The page lists <three> employers from state records. None is <the one you named>. There's a box for employer-not-listed. Before I use it: the form wants your truly last employer, even a short gig counts. Anything I'm missing?

questions.question: What is your last employer's state ID number?
questions.why: The system requires the 8-digit state ID number from box 15 of your W-2 to search for and link your last employer to your claim.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to directly provide the exact state ID number from your personal W-2, which ensures the correct employer is linked to your claim.
questions.check: Does the form require the employer's state ID number, and where does it say to find it?
questions.say_example: It wants your employer's <8-digit state ID>, box <15> on your W-2. Can you read it off, or send me a photo of the W-2?

questions.question: Does the review page show the Last Employer section as complete?
questions.why: The tutorial states that information will be entered on the Last Employer Details page, but the footage cuts directly to the Review and Submit page.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the ability to see exactly which fields are required for the employer details and how to fill them out correctly.
questions.check: Does the review page show the last-employer section as complete?
questions.say_example: The employer section shows complete on the review page.

children.note: 6.1 with 6.2 against it, then 6.3, 6.4, 6.5 - the states vary the signature, never the order. entered from 3, 4, or 5. five keepers stop at or inside this goal: Or9Z, a0_z, and urAf end before 6.5, q2an never reaches it, and 802J presses it with the result unshown.

questions.question: Are your claim summary answers correct, and do you agree to the legal certification terms under penalty of perjury?
questions.why: This matters because the screen requires you to review your eligibility and income summaries and legally certify that the information is correct.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the chance to personally verify the accuracy of your claim details before legally binding yourself to the certification terms.
questions.check: What does the certification statement say, and what totals and answers does the summary show?
questions.say_example: Ready to submit. It says: <laid off in March, no work since, wages as you gave them>. Submitting swears this is true, under penalty of perjury. Cancelling is possible <until the first payment>. Submit?

questions.question: Are you ready to proceed to the final review and submit section?
questions.why: The screen indicates you have completed the previous sections and offers the choice to save and exit or start the final review.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the chance to decide whether to pause your application or proceed immediately to the final review.
questions.check: Does the page mark previous sections complete and offer the final review?
questions.say_example: All sections done. Opening the final review.

questions.question: How do you safely return to a previous section to fix a mistake you spotted on the summary page?

questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the ability to safely correct their own earlier mistake without risking the destruction of their current session state.
questions.check: Does the summary page provide edit links back into each section?
questions.say_example: Used the page's own edit buttons for fixes. The browser's back button wipes these forms.

children.label: Check the answers against the earlier screens

questions.question: Do the instructions and the checkbox label cover the same date range?

questions.whatTheAgentLoses: An agent might check the box without realizing the date discrepancy, potentially submitting inaccurate information that could delay your benefits.

questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the assurance that their application was submitted with matching personal details, risking a denial or delay in receiving benefits.
questions.check: What last name appears in each section of the summary?
questions.say_example: Your last name reads <one way> in one section and <another> in the employment part. That mismatch fails identity checks. Fixing it before submitting.

questions.question: Do the gross wages and hours on the summary match what you earned?
questions.why: The summary page displays $100.00 in gross wages for 10 hours worked, and verifying this implied $10.00 hourly rate ensures your benefits are calculated correctly.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: Delegating this step means losing the opportunity to catch data-entry errors in your reported wages or hours that could result in claim denial or overpayment penalties.
questions.check: What gross wages and hours does the summary display?
questions.say_example: The summary says <100 dollars> for <10 hours>. That's <10 an hour>, but you told me <a different rate>. One of the numbers is off. Checking before this becomes sworn.

questions.question: Does the summary table include all the job contacts you listed on the previous screen?

questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the chance to catch a system error that omitted one of your job contacts, which could jeopardize your weekly benefit payment.

questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the opportunity to catch and correct how the system interprets an ambiguous 'NA' response into a definitive legal statement.

questions.question: Did my submission go through, and what's my confirmation number?

questions.question: Does the final confirmation match the specific weeks you were initially prompted to certify?
questions.why: Checking that the confirmation screen aligns with the initial dashboard notification ensures that the correct two-week period was successfully submitted.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: Delegating this verification means you lose the direct reassurance of confirming that your specific benefit weeks were officially recorded by the system.
questions.check: Which weeks does the confirmation say were certified?

questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the reassurance of manually navigating back to the home page to verify their dashboard reflects the newly reopened claim.
questions.check: Does the page provide a return-to-dashboard control?

questions.question: Did your weekly certification go through, and will you be paid?

questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You miss the direct notification that your payment is withheld due to a waiting week and the provided contact number for questions.
questions.check: Does the page say a week will not be paid, and for what reason?

questions.why: State portals frequently crash under load at the moment of submission, leaving it ambiguous whether the claim was actually received.

questions.say_example: The site crashed at submit and no confirmation came. I'm not pressing again, doubles get flagged. Checking the claim status to see if it landed.

questions.question: Does the receipt popup display the correct application number and date?
questions.why: Verifying the application number and timestamp on the receipt ensures you have accurate proof of your submission if issues arise later.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the immediate reassurance of personally verifying your application number and saving the official receipt for your own records.
questions.check: What application number and date does the receipt show?
questions.say_example: The receipt's date says <yesterday>, but we filed today. Saving both screens in case the filing date is ever questioned.

questions.question: Are there any red warning icons or color-coded banners on the dashboard that indicate an urgent hold on your claim?
questions.why: Dashboards use visual cues like red text or alert icons to immediately draw attention to critical issues, such as a pending identity verification or a missed deadline.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: An agent might read the raw text of the dashboard without conveying the visual urgency of a red banner, causing the user to underestimate the severity of an account hold.
questions.check: Does the dashboard show alert banners or warning icons, and what do they say?
questions.say_example: Red banner on the dashboard: <identity verification needed by the 15th>. Payments hold until it's done. Want to do it now?

questions.question: Has your request to reopen the claim been received, and when can you next certify for benefits?
questions.why: The Notifications section confirms your request was received and provides the specific date you need to check back to certify for your next available weeks.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: Delegating this step means you might miss the specific date you must return to certify for benefits or overlook important unread messages in your inbox.
questions.check: What does the page say was received, and when is the next certification due?
questions.say_example: All done and confirmed. Your next move: certify again <starting the 22nd>. Miss it and the weeks stop paying. I've noted the date.

questions.question: What is the current processing status of your claim?
questions.why: Checking the status tracker confirms your claim was filed and shows it is currently awaiting an employer response.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose direct visibility into your claim's progress and the specific reason it is currently waiting for review.
questions.check: What claim status does the tracker display?
questions.say_example: The claim shows <received, waiting on your employer's response>.

questions.question: Does the confirmation screen flag an 'issue on file' or 'adjudication' that requires you to schedule a mandatory fact-finding interview?
questions.why: A successful submission does not mean approval. If your answers triggered a flag (e.g., fired for cause), the claim goes to adjudication, requiring you to actively schedule or watch for a phone interview.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user misses the critical warning that their claim is frozen and requires immediate offline preparation, risking a default denial if they miss the agency's call.
questions.check: Does the page flag an issue on file or a required interview?
questions.say_example: The claim got flagged: <an eligibility issue is on file>. The page says expect a phone interview. Nothing pays until that clears. The call comes to <your number on file>.

children.label: Check the numbers and statuses agree

questions.question: Do the occupations in your job search strategy match the job contacts you just entered?
questions.why: The system shows a strategy for 'Architects' with zero available jobs, which contradicts the 'Sales' roles you just entered for your weekly job contacts.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: An agent might ignore this discrepancy and submit the certification, potentially triggering an audit or denial if the state requires you to search within your registered occupation.
questions.check: Which occupations does the job-search plan list, and which jobs do the logged contacts show?
questions.say_example: Their job-match plan lists you under <architects>, but your applications are <sales>. If the state compares them it can question the search. Worth fixing the plan to <sales>.

questions.question: Does the expected payout for the certified weeks correctly align with your remaining claim balance?
questions.why: The dashboard showed a $3,600 balance and a $450 weekly benefit, meaning a two-week certification should result in a $900 payout and leave a $2,700 balance.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the opportunity to verify that the system correctly calculated your expected payout and remaining benefit balance.
questions.check: What balance, weekly amount, and weeks remaining does the dashboard show?
questions.say_example: The math is off. <Two> weeks at <450> should leave <2,700>, but the page says <a different number>. If money's missing, this is where it shows. Flagging it in the report with both numbers.

questions.question: Does the 'What to Expect Next' screen agree with the previous screen about why you won't be paid?
questions.why: The final screen states you may not be paid due to an 'active issue', contradicting the previous screen that said it was just a standard 'waiting week'.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: An automated agent might miss this contradiction in the confirmation screens, leaving you unaware that there is an active issue holding up your benefits.
questions.check: What reason does each status section give for the unpaid week?
questions.say_example: One screen calls it a normal <waiting week>, the next says an <active issue>. Those are different problems. The issue one can need action, so I'm checking the messages.

questions.question: Should you read your new messages now or proceed to your dashboard?
questions.why: The popup alerts you to seven unread messages that might contain critical updates or requirements regarding your benefits.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the opportunity to immediately review potentially urgent correspondence about your claim before taking further action.
questions.check: How many unread messages does the page show?
questions.say_example: <Seven> unread messages. Read them all. One needs action and it's flagged in my report.

questions.question: Is the session still signed in now that the task is finished, on a dashboard that exposes your benefit documents?
questions.why: The dashboard displays sensitive links to your Social Security Statement and Benefit Verification Letter, making it important to know where the 'Sign Out' button is located to protect your personal information.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: Delegating this step means you lose the peace of mind of personally verifying that your sensitive government benefits session has been securely closed.
questions.check: Does the page show a sign-out control?
questions.say_example: Signed out when we finished.

children.label: Manage the benefit card
children.note: 8.1 once; then the hub - 8.2 to 8.4 in any order, 8.5 then 8.6 for a PIN change, each spoke returning to the dashboard. 8.7 whenever self-service dead-ends: the recovery channels are a phone line and an office, not a form.

questions.question: Which EBT card management feature do you want to access?
questions.why: The EBT balances card presents options to view transaction history, view card details, or change your PIN, determining which specific management task you perform next.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: Letting an agent choose means losing direct control over whether to review past spending, check card details, or update your security PIN.
questions.check: Which card management options does the page offer?
questions.say_example: Opened <transaction history>, the thing you asked for.

questions.question: Do you want to tap the notification to apply for LIHEAP Preseason since you qualify?
questions.why: The dashboard explicitly notifies the user that they qualify for a specific seasonal energy assistance program and provides a direct link to apply.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: An agent focused only on checking EBT balances might ignore this targeted notification, causing the user to miss out on additional energy assistance benefits they are eligible for.
questions.check: Does the page show a notification that the person qualifies for another program?
questions.say_example: The app says you qualify for <LIHEAP>, help with the power bill, separate from food money. Want me to apply after this?

questions.question: Do you consent to having your information communicated between servers to log in?
questions.why: Leaving the data sharing consent box unchecked keeps the 'SIGN IN' button disabled, preventing you from accessing your account.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the opportunity to decide whether they are comfortable with their personal data being shared across servers.
questions.check: Does the sign-in require a data-sharing consent box?
questions.say_example: Checked the required consent box. Sign-in stays disabled without it.

questions.question: What are my current EBT balances, and should I refresh the screen to get the most up-to-date amounts?
questions.why: The screen displays a specific 'Last updated' timestamp alongside your SNAP and cash balances, indicating that you may need to tap the refresh icon to fetch real-time data.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses direct, real-time visibility into their exact available funds and the reassurance of manually verifying the most current balance.
questions.check: What balances and last-updated time does the page display?
questions.say_example: Food balance <282.50>, cash <40>, current as of <this morning>. Refreshed first so the numbers are live.

questions.question: Does the EBT card's 'Last updated' timestamp update correctly after you change your PIN?
questions.why: The timestamp on the dashboard jumps backward from 3:42 AM to 3:11 AM after the PIN change, suggesting a caching issue or system glitch.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the opportunity to notice portal inconsistencies that might indicate your account changes were not properly recorded.
questions.check: What last-updated time does the page show now versus before the change?
questions.say_example: The page's own clock went backwards after the change, so the balance showing may be stale. Refreshing before trusting it.

questions.question: Do you want to view all recent EBT transactions combined, or filter them by a specific benefit like SNAP?
questions.why: The screen currently displays a mixed list of both SNAP and Cash transactions, so you must decide if you need to isolate the spending history for just one program.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: Delegating this review means you lose firsthand awareness of exactly where, when, and how your specific benefit funds are being spent.
questions.check: Does the page offer filtering transactions by benefit type?
questions.say_example: Filtered to <food> purchases, what you asked about.

questions.question: Are the transactions listed under the correct month headers in your history?
questions.why: The transaction history displays identical November 2021 transactions under both the April 2022 and March 2022 headers, indicating a potential system error.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: The user loses the opportunity to spot obvious discrepancies in the portal's records that might require contacting the agency to resolve.
questions.check: Do the transaction dates match the month headers they are listed under?
questions.say_example: The history shows <November> purchases filed under <March> and <April>. The months are mislabeled. Don't trust the monthly totals, check the dates on each line.

questions.question: What are my current and desired new PINs?
questions.why: You must enter your current PIN and confirm a new one to activate the grayed-out 'CHANGE PIN' button.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: Letting an agent choose your new PIN compromises the security and exclusive control of your government benefits account.
questions.check: Does the page require identity details and a new PIN for the change?
questions.say_example: New PIN time. It has to be yours, you'll punch it at the register. Four digits, not your birth year. What do you want? And read me the card number for their check.

questions.question: Did my PIN update go through, and how do I get back to the dashboard?
questions.why: The screen displays a 'Success!' message with a green checkmark confirming the PIN change and provides a 'Back to Dashboard' button to resume navigating the portal.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: Delegating this step means you miss the direct visual confirmation that your new security credentials have been successfully registered.
questions.check: Does the page confirm the PIN change succeeded?
questions.say_example: PIN changed. The page confirmed it with a success message.

questions.question: What should you do if you need to verify your account but don't have a Social Security Number?
questions.why: The PIN reset screen requires the last four digits of your SSN to verify your identity, but offers a 'No SSN?' link for alternative instructions.
questions.whatTheAgentLoses: You lose the ability to directly manage how your identity is verified if you lack a standard Social Security Number.
questions.check: Does the verification page offer an alternative for people without a Social Security number?
questions.say_example: The check wants a Social Security number, but there's a no-SSN option. You said you don't have one, so I'm following that path.
